summary.text: 南 is attested for “south” in Shang inscriptions. Its early graph’s depicted object remains disputed, and the received Shuowen component analysis is rejected in a consulted modern reference.

formation.text: The early graph has been interpreted as a hanging percussion instrument, a house front, or a covered vessel with a plant-like feature; its referent is unsettled. The received Shuowen account divides it into 𣎵 and phonetic 𢆉, but that component analysis is disputed and does not establish the graph’s original construction.

components.text: One disputed proposal reads the whole early graph as a hanging percussion instrument; other accounts identify it as a house front or covered vessel. No interpretation is settled.
The received Shuowen account assigns 𣎵 a meaning-bearing role in 南. This historical analysis is disputed and does not establish the graph’s original construction.
The received Shuowen account calls 𢆉 phonetic in 南. This historical analysis is disputed; no suitable historical sound comparison here independently confirms that role.

sound_limitation.text: The current Mandarin readings can be compared, but they do not establish that 𢆉 had a phonetic role in 南 historically.

sound.text: These are current Mandarin readings; their comparison documents present pronunciation only.

history.text: Oracle-bone, bronze, manuscript, and seal forms are reported, and the received dictionary tradition records 𡴖 as an ancient form. Later accounts describe graphic changes and confusion with 市-like forms, but do not establish a continuous derivation from any particular Shang object picture.

Shang inscriptions use 南 for the direction, in the ancestor name 南庚, and for a sacrificial item. One account proposes that the graph was borrowed for “south,” but the early object’s identity, name, and pronunciation remain unresolved. These reported uses do not establish which came first or that the directional word was borrowed from an object-name.

uncertainties.text: The early graph’s referent is disputed: proposals include an instrument, a house front, and a covered vessel, among others. The received Shuowen component analysis is also disputed. A proposed lexical link between “south” and a belly or front-of-body word concerns the spoken word’s history; it does not establish how the graph was formed.
The exact earliest inscription and the order of the reported Shang uses are unresolved; a continuous graphic derivation is also not established.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone inscriptions; exact earliest specimen date unresolved
senses.text: 南 is reported for the direction “south” in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions; the exact earliest specimen date is unresolved. This attested use does not establish the graph’s original meaning.

limitations.text: The reported ancestor-name and sacrificial-item uses do not establish separate character senses or a chronology among the Shang uses.

Instrument-name borrowing is a proposal, not a verified explanation: the proposed instrument’s identity, ancient name, and pronunciation are unresolved, and the reported Shang uses do not establish that the directional word was borrowed from its name.
The proposed lexical link between “south” and a belly or front-of-body word does not establish a semantic development.

relationships.text: This disputed analysis treats the whole early graph as an object picture; competing interpretations identify different objects.
The received Shuowen analysis assigns 𣎵 a semantic role in 南. This historical interpretation is disputed and does not establish the graph’s original construction.
The received Shuowen analysis calls 𢆉 phonetic in 南. Its current Mandarin reading can be compared with 南 nán, but this does not independently confirm the proposed historical phonetic role.

overview.text: 南 means ‘south,’ a meaning attested in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions and used in present-day Mandarin. The early graph’s referent and construction remain disputed.

limitations.text: No usable glyph image is available to illustrate 南’s early forms: the identified oracle, seal, and ancient-script images are modern redraws, and the original image files could not be retrieved. Their labels and historical accounts do not establish what object, if any, the early graph depicted; that interpretation remains disputed.
